'''Bunuba''' (Bunaba, Bunapa, Punuba, Punapa, Punaba, Buniba) is an [[Australian Aboriginal languages|Australian Aboriginal language]] spoken by some 41 older [[Bunuba]] adults, most of whom live in [[Junjuwa community|Junjuwa]], an Aboriginal community in [[Fitzroy Crossing]] in [[Western Australia]].<ref>{{Cite web|last=Anonymous|date=2019-07-26|title=K5: Bunuba|url=https://collection.aiatsis.gov.au/austlang/language/k5|access-date=2022-01-04|website=collection.aiatsis.gov.au|language=en}}</ref> Bunuba is not related to the [[Pama–Nyungan languages|Pama-Nyungan language family]] that spans the majority of Australia; however, it is a relative of [[Guniyandi language|Guniyandi]]. Both are subgroups of the [[Bunuban languages|Bunuban language family]].<ref name=":0">{{Cite book|title=Cross-Linguistic Semantics|url=https://archive.org/details/crosslinguistics00godd|url-access=limited|last=Knight|first=Emily|publisher=John Benjamins Publishing Company|year=2008|isbn=9789027205698|editor-last=Goddard|editor-first=Cliff|location=Amsterdam, Netherlands|pages=[https://archive.org/details/crosslinguistics00godd/page/n222 206]|chapter=7. Hyperpolysemy in Bunuba, a Polysynthetic Language of the Kimberley, Western Australia}}</ref> Bunuba consists of two dialects, 'light' and 'heavy' Bunuba.<ref name=":3" /><ref name=":5" />

Due to the growing concern of their language becoming extinct, the elders to maintain the use of Bunuba by passing on stories to younger community members around campfires at night. This is a way for Bunuba elders to prevent the extinction of their language, by passing it down through generations.<ref>{{Citation|title=Language: Bunuba, Australia|url=http://www.unesco.org/archives/multimedia/document-1771|access-date=2019-06-29}}</ref> Language maintenance and revival has increased during the later decades of the 20th century and the early 21st century due to the growing documentation of Bunuba language, and the production of resources that have been written and used by Bunuba community members.

== History of research on Bunuba ==

=== Early phase (late 19th century – 1929) ===
The first distinctions made between the [[Australian Aboriginal languages]] of the north and south of Australia were by [[Wilhelm Schmidt (linguist)]] in 1919.<ref name=":1">{{Cite book|last=McGregor|first=William B.|title=The Languages of the Kimberley, Western australia|publisher=Routledge|year=2004|author-link = William B. McGregor}}</ref> These language groups later became known as [[Pama–Nyungan languages|Pama–Nyungan]] (the Southern languages) and [[Non-Pama-Nyungan]] (the Northern Languages).<ref name=":0" />

=== Intermediate phase (1930–1959) ===
From 1938 to 1989 Australian linguist, [[Arthur Capell]] visited the [[Northern Territory]] to record features of Kimberley Languages including Bunuba.<ref name=":1"/> Capell's studies were published in 1940 in the journal article ''The Classification of Languages in North and North-West Australia''.<ref name=":4">{{Cite journal|last=Capell|first=Arthur|date=1940|title=The Classification of Languages in North and North-West Australia|journal=Oceania|volume=10|issue=4|pages=404–433|doi=10.1002/j.1834-4461.1940.tb00304.x|author-link=Arthur Capell}}</ref> His written work is now located at Canberra's [[Australian Institute of Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Studies]]. ''A New Approach to Australian Linguistics'' published by Capell in 1956 details the classifications and typologies of [[Australian Aboriginal languages]], including those of the [[Kimberley (Western Australia)]].<ref name=":2">{{Cite book|last=Capell|first=Arthur|title=A New Approach to Australian Linguistics|publisher=University of Sydney}}</ref>

=== Modern phase (1960 – present) ===
The modern phase of Australian Aboriginal Language research employs a [[Linguistic description|descriptive]] approach that is [[grammar]]-oriented.<ref name=":1"/> Howard Coate documented Bunuba in the mid-1960s, applying new approaches and modern linguistic research methods to his contributions.<ref name=":1"/> In particular, he produced audio recordings of Bunuba dialogue which is also now located at the [[Australian Institute of Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Studies]].<ref name=":2"/> Australian linguist Alan Rumsey has extensively contributed to detailed linguistic coverage of Bunuba from the 1970s until the 1990s whilst working with the local Bunuba community.<ref name=":3">{{Cite book|last=Knight|first=Emily|title=Aspects of Bunuba grammar and semantics|publisher=Armidale: University of New England|year=2004}}</ref> Rumsey has focused on [[syntax]] and producing a Bunuba [[grammar]]; notably [[phonology]], [[Morphology (linguistics)|morphology]], and the person/number system.

== Classification ==
Bunuba is a [[Non-Pama-Nyungan]] language and a subgroup of the [[Bunuban languages|Bunuban family languages]].<ref name=":5">{{Cite book|last=Rumsey|first=Alan|title=The Handbook of Australian Languages Volume 5|publisher=Oxford|editor-last=Dixon|editor-first=R.M.W|pages=35–154|chapter=Bunuba|editor-last2=Blake|editor-first2=B. J.}}</ref> It is not related to the [[Pama–Nyungan languages]] that span the majority of Australia.<ref name=":3" />

=== Arthur Capell's classification ===
Capell classified Bunuba as a non-classifying language of the [[Fitzroy River (Western Australia)|Fitzroy]] basin region, alongside [[Guniyandi language|Guniyandi.]]<ref name=":4" /> Bunuba is non-classifying in that it does not rely on the use of [[noun class]]es nor [[grammatical gender]].<ref name=":1" /> For example, Bunuba does not have gendered [[pronoun]]s, rather it uses a singular 'they' pronoun {{Lang|bck|niyiŋga}} for third-person singular 'he', 'she', and 'it'.<ref>{{Cite web|last=Greenhill|first=S|date=2021|title=Language: Bunuba|url=http://pdb.simon.net.nz/language/bunuba|url-status=live|website=Pronoun Paradigms Database|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220104075715/http://pdb.simon.net.nz/language/bunuba |archive-date=4 January 2022 }}</ref>

== Related languages ==
[[File:A Map of Bunuba Country.jpg|thumb|400x400px]]
Bunuba Country is surrounded by other [[Non-Pama-Nyungan]] speaking regions of [[Guniyandi language|Guniyandi]], [[Gija language|Gija]], [[Ngarinyin language|Ngarinyin]], [[Nyigina language|Nyigina]], [[Unggumi language|Unggumi]], and [[Warrwa language|Warrwa]].<ref name=":2" /> Their similarity to Bunuba was determined by comparing how many words each languages shared with [[Kenneth L. Hale]]'s list of 100 foundational words of Northern Paman languages.<ref name=":1" /><ref name=":2" />

=== Relationship to Guniyandi ===
Although [[Guniyandi language|Guniyandi]] is the most similar language to Bunuba based on [[linguistic typology]], they are not [[mutually intelligible]], rather they are subgroups of the overarching [[Bunuban languages|Bunuban family]] language group.<ref name=":1" /> Based on Hale's list of 100 foundational words, approximately 45% of Bunuba vocabulary is shared with Guniyandi; this percentage determines their relationship as subgroups of the larger language group.<ref name=":1" />

== Dialect variation ==
There are two regional Bunuba [[dialect]]s which are distinguished based on where they are geographically spoken within Bunuba Country.<ref name=":3" /> In the eastern and southern regions of Bunuba Country, a 'light' Bunuba dialect if spoken.<ref name=":5" /> In the northern and western regions a 'heavy' dialect is used, which is also known as ''Unggumi Bunuba'' in reference to the similarities that it shares with [[Unggumi language]] spoken by the [[Unggumi|Unggumi peoples]] in the region north-west of Bunuba Country.<ref name=":3" /><ref name=":5" />

The main contrast between light and heavy Bunuba dialects is based on the phonological differences that are characteristic of Unggumi.<ref name=":5" /> For example, the light Bunuba dialect utilises a /y/ phoneme in place of /yh/ which is more common in the heavy dialect.<ref name=":5" /> This variation is present in dialectal differences between the words for 'meat' with light dialect speakers utilising /{{lang|bck|miya}}/ and heavy dialect speakers adhering to the older pronunciation of /{{lang|bck|miyha}}/. The use of /y/ and /yh/ causes /miya/ and /{{lang|bck|miyha}}/ to become a [[minimal pair]].<ref name=":3" /><ref name=":5" /> Generally, Bunuba dialectal differences do not present problems in understanding between speakers of each dialect.<ref name=":3" />

==== Stops and nasals ====
Bunuba, like some of its neighbouring [[Kimberley (Western Australia)|Kimberley]] languages, has six [[Articulatory phonetics|articulation]] points that determine the articulatory differences between [[Plosive|stops]] and [[Nasal consonant|nasals]].<ref name=":1" /> These are [[Bilabial consonant|bilabial]] articulation, [[Velar consonant|velar]] articulation, [[Dental consonant|dental]] articulation, [[Palatal consonant|palatal]] articulation, [[Alveolar consonant|alveolar]] articulation, and [[Retroflex consonant|retroflex]] articulation.<ref name=":1" /> These are grouped together into more general places of articulation based on tongue placement. Bilabial and velar articulations are grouped together as [[Peripheral consonant|peripherals]] because their pronunciation requires articulation at the front and back peripheries of the mouth.<ref name=":1" /> Dental and palatal articulations are groups under [[Laminal consonant|laminals]] as they utilise the larger central body of the tongue during pronunciation.<ref name=":1" /> Alveolar and retroflex are grouped as [[Apical consonant|apicals]] because they use the tongue tip.<ref name=":1" />

Word initial stops are either [[Voice (phonetics)|voiced]] or [[Aspirated consonant|non-aspirated]] and [[Voicelessness|voiceless]].<ref name=":5" /> They are also fully voiced when they occur in any other place in a word.<ref name=":5" /> In words that are expressively or emotionally emphasised, the stop can become aspirated.<ref name=":5" /> For example, when a mother firmly addresses her son with 'son' [{{lang|bck|‘cʰukʰu}}].<ref name=":5" />

==== Laterals ====
Bunuba utilises three [[Lateral consonant|laterals]] that are common to almost all Kimberley languages: {{grapheme|l}}, {{grapheme|rl}}, and {{grapheme|ly}}.<ref name=":1" /> For all three, the tip of the tongue touches the roof of the mouth.<ref name=":5" /> The distinguishing articulatory factor is the larger central body of the tongue, which is situated low for {{grapheme|rl}}, central for {{grapheme|l}} and high for {{grapheme|ly}}.(rum) {{IPAblink|ɭ}} {{grapheme|rl}} is depicted as {{grapheme|l}} in Bunuba orthography.<ref name=":5" />

Examples of lateral contrasts:<ref name=":5" />

* {{Lang|bck|balarra}} 'outside'
* {{Lang|bck|walarri}} 'ghost gum, snappy gum'
* {{Lang|bck|walyarra}} 'sand'

==== Rhotics ====
Bunuba has two [[Rhotic consonant|rhotic]] sounds.

# {{grapheme|rr}} {{IPAblink|r}} the [[alveolar tap]], similar to the [[Trill consonant|trill]] present in [[Scottish English]].<ref name=":5" /><ref name=":1" />
# {{grapheme|r}} {{IPAblink|ɻ}} the [[Retroflex consonant|retroflex continuant]] which is akin to other [[English dialects]] which utilise a continuant r-sound.<ref name=":1" /> The tongue does not touch the roof of the mouth.<ref name=":5" />

==== Glides ====
The Bunuba {{IPAblink|w}} and {{IPAblink|j}} are akin to English pronunciations of {{grapheme|w}} and {{grapheme|y}} respectively.<ref name=":1" /> The pronunciation of the [[Dental consonant|dental glide]] {{grapheme|yh}} requires a lateral spreading of the tongue, with an articulatory point similar to those of {{grapheme|nh}} and {{grapheme|th}}.<ref name=":5" /> This glide is unique to Bunuba and the neighbouring language of [[Unggumi]].<ref name=":5" /> It is also the distinguishing factor between light and heavy Bunuba dialects.

=== Vowels ===
Bunuba has only three basic vowel phonemes: /i, a, u/.

/a/ is the only vowel demonstrating contrastive [[vowel length]].<ref name=":3" />

== Grammar ==

=== Parts of Speech ===

==== Nominals ====
[[Nominal (linguistics)|Nominals]] in Bunuba are free [[lexeme]]s which [[morpheme]]s can be added to.<ref name=":5" /> This is central to its distinction as a polysynthetic language.

'''Verbal words'''

Bunuba [[verb]]s contain [[affix]]es; a [[preverb]], and an [[Auxiliary verb|auxiliary]].<ref name=":5" /> Depending on the verb, the two affixes can take on individual word meanings, or add meaning to the root verb.<ref name=":5" />

'''Adverbs'''

Bunuba [[adverb]]s are not the same as aforementioned verbal words, as they are standalone words which affixes cannot be added on to.<ref name=":5" />

'''Pronouns'''

[[Pronoun]]s contain numeric distinctions in the root of the word.<ref name=":5" />

'''Kin terms'''

Bunuba [[kin term]]s are [[Vocative case|vocative]], take on [[Inflection|possessive inflections]], and possess a [[Numeral (linguistics)|number system]].<ref name=":5" />

=== Reduplication ===
Bunuba utilises [[reduplication]] to indicate plurality.<ref name=":1" /> Bunuba uses both partial and total reduplication.<ref name=":1" /> Partial reduplication requires a repetition of only a certain part of the root word, whilst total reduplication uses a repetition of the whole root word.<ref name=":1" />

For example:<ref name=":1" />

* In reference to a group of children: {{Lang|bck|ma-mabilyi}} 'little ones' stemming from {{Lang|bck|mabilyi}} 'little'
* In reference to the husbands of multiple women: {{Lang|bck|nhungu-nhungu-way}} 'their husbands' stemming from {{Lang|bck|nhungu-way}} 'her husband'

Reduplication is also used in Bunuba to intensify words.<ref name=":1" />

For example:<ref name=":1" />

* {{Lang|bck|gililandirri}} 'very big' stemming from {{Lang|bck|gilandirri}} 'big'

== Typology ==

=== Morphological Typology ===
Bunuba is a [[polysynthetic language]]; words consist of multiple morphemes, which can also have meanings independent of their position in a polysynthetic word.<ref name=":5" />

== Documentation and revival ==

=== Kimberley Language Resource Centre ===
The Kimberley Language Resource Centre (KLRC) was established in 1984 with the role of revitalising, maintaining, and promoting [[Australian Aboriginal languages]].<ref name=":6">{{Cite web|title=KLRC {{!}} About|url=https://klrc.org.au/about/|access-date=2022-01-04|language=en-AU}}</ref>

==== Community engagement ====
A main aim of KLRC is to assist with career opportunities that cater to the cross-cultural and language needs of Kimberley language groups.<ref name=":6"/> This is done by providing training for community members of language groups in order to increase chances of employment in sectors that can cater to their linguistic needs.<ref name=":6"/>

==== Bunuba orthography ====
Prior to 1989, linguistic research on Bunuba has not followed a specific orthography, leading to possible discrepancies between [[lexical item]]s. To improve linguistic clarity, KLRC assisted approximately twenty local Bunuba speakers in producing an [[orthography]] for the language in 1989.<ref name=":5" /> The orthography was then utilised in 1991 to create an illustrated Bunuba wordbook that continues to be used in the teaching and learning of the language.<ref name=":5" />

==== Written, audio, and video documentation ====
KLRC owns archives of linguistic material from the 1950s until present, that have been provided by Australian linguists and language workers who have researched Aboriginal languages of the [[Kimberley (Western Australia)|Kimberley]] Region.<ref name=":5" /> Apart from storing archival material at the resource centre, KLRC works alongside the [[Australian Institute of Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Studies]] (AIATSIS) to return language resources back to Indigenous communities.<ref name=":6"/> Resources include documentation from Howard Coate's research on Bunuban languages.<ref name=":5" /> To increase the revitalisation and maintenance of Bunuba, KLRC owns archival documents of the language in audio, video, and book formats.<ref>Kimberley Language Resource Centre. (2020). ''Strategic Plan August 2020 Consultation Draft.'' Kimberley Language Resource Centre. https://klrc.org.au/wp-content/uploads/2020/10/KLRC-Strategic-Plan-August-2020-consultation-draft.pdf</ref>

===== ''Thangani Bunuba'' (''Bunuba Stories'') =====
''Thangani Bunuba'' is a collection of stories told by twelve Bunuba elders from the Fitzroy River region.<ref name=":7">Kimberley Language Resource Centre. (1998). ''Thangani Bunuba: Bunuba Stories''. Kimberley Language Resource Centre.</ref> The creation of this book was a project that aimed to revive and maintain the Bunuba language and was undertaken at the request of the Bunuba elders who sought after a way for the language to be preserved.<ref name=":7" /> The elders worked alongside linguists and language workers from the KLRC in order to translate the stories into English.<ref name=":7" />

Stories were shared by the elders alongside the traditional paintings that are featured in the book.<ref name=":7"/> The process of creating this book required audio recordings of each story to be produced, which were able to be transcribed and later translated into English by Bunuba speakers and linguists.<ref name=":7"/> The book also contains a 'Guide to Bunuba Pronunciation' which consists of an orthography of Bunuba with a phonetic assistance based on English pronunciation of the same vowels and consonants.<ref name=":7"/>

== Bunuba in theatre ==

=== The Story of Jandamarra ===
[[Jandamarra]] was an [[Aboriginal Australians|Aboriginal Australian]] man and a leader of the Bunuba people throughout the late 1800s.<ref name=":8">{{Citation|last=Pedersen|first=Howard|title=Jandamarra (1870–1897)|url=https://adb.anu.edu.au/biography/jandamarra-8822|work=Australian Dictionary of Biography|place=Canberra|publisher=National Centre of Biography, Australian National University|language=en|access-date=2022-01-10}}</ref> Due to his proficiency in English he had a range of occupations including working for local police by looking after their horses.<ref name=":8" /> Jandamarra became a [[Stockman (Australia)|stockman]] at Lillimooloora station, and was later employed as an [[Aboriginal tracker]] to assist in capturing Bunuba people.<ref name=":8" /> He is mostly known for his role in organising and leading resistance against European settlers in the southern areas of the [[Kimberley Region]].<ref name=":8" /> Jandamarra's biography has been reproduced in different entertainment media formats, such as the 2008 stage play ''Jandamarra'' by Bunuba Films which included dialogue in Bunuba language.

==== Jandamarra (stage play) ====
The production of the 2008 stage play was based on the 1995 historical book ''Jandamarra and the Bunuba Resistance'' written in collaboration between historian Howard Pedersen and Bunuba elder Banjo Woorunmurra, of whom the story of Jandamarra was under senior custodianship.<ref name=":11">{{Cite web|title=Jandamarra - Bunuba Films|url=http://www.jandamarra.com.au/bunubafilms.html|access-date=2022-01-10|website=www.jandamarra.com.au}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|title=Howard Pedersen|url=https://www.magabala.com/collections/howard-pedersen|access-date=2022-01-10|website=Magabala Books|language=en}}</ref> The story of Jandamarra was adapted into the stage play ''Jandamarra'' which was produced by the Bunuba run company, Bunuba Films in co-production with the [[Black Swan State Theatre Company]].<ref name=":11" /><ref name=":9">{{Cite web|title=Jandamarra - The Play|url=http://www.jandamarra.com.au/theplay.html|access-date=2022-01-10|website=www.jandamarra.com.au}}</ref> The stage play went on tour as The Jandamarra Returns Tour (2011) which ran from July to August, with thirteen performances altogether.<ref name=":10">{{Cite web|title=Jandamarra - The Yilimbirri Junba|url=http://www.jandamarra.com.au/tour.html|access-date=2022-01-10|website=www.jandamarra.com.au}}</ref> Tour locations included Broome, Kununurra, Lundja Community of Halls Creek, and Windjana Gorge, amassing 5,097 total audience members.<ref name=":10" />

To immerse audiences into the Bunuban storyline, a conscious decision was made by playwright, Steve Hawke to use Bunuba language and [[Australian Kriol|Kimberley Kriol]] for scenes that were situated in the Bunuban environment.<ref name=":9" /> Linguists and language coaches were appointed during workshops arranged by the collaborating Bunuba Films and the Black Swan State Theatre company, between March and April 2007.<ref name=":9" /> Bunuba language was integrated into the script through the work of four Bunuba women of linguistic and community leadership backgrounds: Mona Oscar, Patsy Bedford, [[June Oscar]], and Selina Middleton.<ref name=":9" /> They worked as translators to provide the [[back translation]]s for [[surtitles]]. The script was translated from English into Bunuba, then translated back into English by the group of translators who ensured the maintenance of cultural salience.<ref name=":9" /> The [[back translation]]s were then projected onto a screen as [[surtitles]] for audiences to understand the scenes which depicted Bunuba language, culture, and country.<ref name=":9" /> Bunuba elders taught the language to the actors, with lead actor, Damion Hunter undergoing Bunuba language coaching during the production phase in order to depict the main role of Jandamarra.<ref name=":10" /> The use of Bunuba language included the performance of ''{{lang|bck|Yilimbirri Junba}},'' a traditional song and dance carried out by Bunuba singers, dancers, and lawmen.<ref>{{Cite news|last=Laurie|first=Victoria|date=January 31, 2008|title=Warrior's Language of Resistance|page=14|work=The Australian|url=http://www.jandamarra.com.au/WarriorsLanguageArticle.pdf|access-date=January 8, 2022}}</ref>
